title: How to Create a Monthly Budget
excerpt: Build a monthly household budget using take-home income, essential expenses, and realistic Pakistani Rupee savings targets.
introduction: A budget helps you decide what your money needs to do before you spend it. Start with the month ahead, use real take-home numbers, and leave room to adjust for seasonal utilities and groceries. All figures below are illustrative Pakistani Rupee (PKR) examples, not rigid spending prescriptions.
author: HisabKi Kitab Editorial Team

blocks.text: When salary arrives on the 1st, a healthy bank balance can create a false sense of security. But when house rent, electricity bills (LESCO/K-Electric), school fees, and ration expenses arrive at staggered dates throughout the month, unbudgeted spending early on leads to cash shortages before the next payday.

Separate money committed to essential obligations from money available for flexible day-to-day spending. Base your plan on net take-home pay rather than gross salary before taxes and deductions. For families and individuals in Pakistan, an adapted 50/30/20 guideline works well: 50–60% for non-negotiable household essentials (ration, rent, utilities), 20–30% for variable living costs, and 10–20% for emergency savings or debt payoff.

Ayesha manages a household with PKR 100,000 net monthly take-home income. She sets aside funds for rent, monthly ration, utilities, transport, and a dedicated emergency reserve before assigning her flexible spending limit.

blocks.caption: Illustrative monthly allocation in Pakistani Rupees (PKR)

blocks.text: PKR 100,000 Net Income − (32,000 + 24,000 + 12,000 + 8,000 + 6,000 + 10,000 Committed Costs) = PKR 8,000 available for discretionary spending across the month.

items: List confirmed take-home pay and the exact dates it clears into your account.
Ring-fence committed expenses: rent, utility bills, school fees, and ration.
Transfer a predetermined savings percentage (minimum 10%) immediately at payday before spending.
Divide your discretionary allowance across 4 weeks so you do not run out of funds mid-month.
Conduct a 10-minute weekly review to compare actual receipts against your planned categories.
Treating a revolving committee (kameti) payout as fresh income rather than disciplined past savings.
Forgetting periodic annual bills such as vehicle token taxes, Eid shopping, or school admissions.
Setting daily food or commute estimates too low to realistically follow in an inflationary environment.
Relying on credit cards or informal borrowing to bridge recurring monthly spending gaps.

blocks.text: Managing seasonal utility spikes in Pakistan

Summer air conditioning and winter gas charges cause dramatic bill fluctuations. Look at your past 12 months of utility bills, calculate the monthly average, and save a small utility cushion during mild spring and autumn months to absorb peak billing seasons.

Your first budget is a baseline estimate, not a permanent constraint. A practical budget becomes more accurate through regular weekly reviews and honest category adjustments, giving you full control over your financial future.

faqs.question: What is the best way to make a monthly salary budget in Pakistan? (Salary ka budget kaise banayein?)
faqs.answer: Start with your confirmed net take-home pay. Ring-fence 50-60% for essential household costs (rent, ration, utilities), reserve at least 10% for savings, and divide the remaining balance across 4 weeks for day-to-day out-of-pocket expenses.

faqs.question: How should I handle rising electricity and utility bills in my budget?
faqs.answer: Track your utility bills across summer and winter seasons. Set aside a 10-15% utility buffer during moderate weather months to absorb peak summer electricity surcharges without breaking your monthly grocery plan.

faqs.question: How often should I review my monthly budget?
faqs.answer: A short 10-minute weekly review helps you identify overspending early, while a full monthly reconciliation at payday allows you to adjust category limits for the upcoming month.
